Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery

Unexpected admissions after planned outpatient non-melanoma skin cancer reconstruction: Risk factors and a bedside risk score

Schaschinger T, Marcela FO, Niederegger T et al. · 2026 Oct 09
Study Type: Retrospective cohort study (ACS-NSQIP database, 2008–2023) with risk score derivation.
Key Question: What factors predict unexpected admission or prolonged observation after planned outpatient NMSC reconstruction, and can a simple bedside score stratify this risk?
Key Findings:
  • Of 5,371 patients, 779 (14.5%, ~1 in 7) required unexpected admission.
  • Strongest independent associations: operative complexity (regional myocutaneous flap aOR 7.59; free flap/nodal/salivary or bone resection aOR 20.76), general anaesthesia (local/MAC associated with substantially lower odds), higher ASA grade, chronic corticosteroid use, and dependent functional status.
  • The integer score had an AUC of 0.778 (full model 0.789, well calibrated) and stratified admission risk from 2.0% (score ≤0) to 79.0% (≥10).
Clinical Relevance: The score could support preoperative triage, bed planning and anaesthetic choice for day-case skin cancer reconstruction in NHS units.
Limitations: US data with no external or UK validation; NSQIP captures limited procedural and social detail, and "postoperative NMSC diagnosis" and the admission outcome may not map onto UK day-case pathways.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Clinical Outcomes of Submuscular vs Subglandular Implant Placement in Primary Cosmetic Breast Augmentation: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

Cao Q, Zhu L, Zhou F et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (12 studies, n=4534; predominantly observational), PROSPERO-registered.
Key Question: In primary cosmetic breast augmentation, how do submuscular/dual-plane and subglandular implant placement compare for complications and patient-reported outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • Submuscular/dual-plane placement had lower odds of overall complications (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.38-0.62), capsular contracture (OR 0.58, 0.38-0.87), hematoma (OR 0.30, 0.15-0.58) and malposition/asymmetry (OR 0.25, 0.07-0.91).
  • No significant difference in reoperation (OR 0.80, 0.55-1.15) or patient satisfaction (OR 1.00, 0.34-2.96).
  • Sensitivity analyses supported the primary findings.
Clinical Relevance: Supports a lower complication profile for submuscular/dual-plane pockets in primary augmentation, though pocket choice should remain individualised, particularly given patient-specific concerns about animation deformity.
Limitations: Predominantly observational data with no pooled data for animation deformity, pain or envelope-related aesthetics, precluding causal conclusions and a full risk-benefit comparison.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Is a Higher Modified Frailty Index Associated with Increased Complications in Breast Reduction? A Single Center Retrospective Analysis of 1716 Patients

Virkalahti J, Laitala M, Giordano S · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Single-centre retrospective cohort study (n=1,716; 2005–2024).
Key Question: Does the five-factor modified Frailty Index (mFI-5) independently predict 30-day complications after bilateral breast reduction?
Key Findings:
  • Unadjusted complication rate was higher in high-frailty (mFI-5 ≥2, n=127) than low-frailty patients (22.2% vs 14.9%; p=0.031), including wound dehiscence, haemorrhage requiring transfusion and nipple-areola complex necrosis.
  • After multivariable adjustment, mFI-5 was not an independent predictor (OR 1.20, 95% CI 0.62–2.33; p=0.588).
  • Independent predictors were higher BMI (OR 1.09 per unit; p=0.007) and active smoking (OR 1.68; p=0.008).
Clinical Relevance: Supports prioritising BMI and smoking cessation optimisation over frailty scoring when counselling and selecting patients for NHS breast reduction.
Limitations: Small high-frailty group (n=127) and retrospective single-centre design limit statistical power and generalisability, and mFI-5 may not capture frailty adequately in a predominantly younger cohort.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Vector Matters: A Critical Review of Biomechanics, Safety, and Evidence Quality in Aesthetic Rib Remodeling

Perez ME, Hoyos AE, Oñate C et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Structured narrative review (January 2015–June 2026); no PRISMA-style counts, extraction sheets or pooled denominator retained.
Key Question: How do parallel corticotomy, perpendicular puncture and rib-resection approaches to aesthetic rib remodelling compare for safety, and how robust is the supporting evidence?
Key Findings:
  • The literature is mainly uncontrolled observational reports, with heterogeneous selection, cointerventions, techniques, surveillance and follow-up, and possibly overlapping cohorts.
  • Parallel-technique cohorts report fewer major pleural events than some perpendicular-technique series, but there is no head-to-head or adjusted comparison, so no causal safety advantage is established.
  • Recent RibXcar reports include pulmonary function, imaging, complications (including fatalities) and patient-reported outcomes, but cohort overlap cannot be excluded. Ultrasound may aid localisation and documentation; its incremental safety benefit is unproven.
Clinical Relevance: Surgeons or patients in the UK considering rib remodelling, including those seeking it abroad, should regard claims of technique-specific safety as unproven when counselling and consenting.
Limitations: No quantitative synthesis or reproducible screening data, with fatalities reported but no verified unique-patient denominator to estimate risk.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Multimodal Scar Prevention Using Botulinum Toxin Type A, Fractional CO2 Laser, and Topical Silicone: A Randomized Split-Scar Clinical Trial

Al-Madhagy G, Hamadah O, Darwich K · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Randomised, assessor-blinded split-scar trial (n=36)
Key Question: Does combining botulinum toxin A, fractional CO2 laser and topical silicone improve scar outcomes compared with dual-modality regimens or silicone alone?
Key Findings:
  • At 6 months, triple therapy gave the lowest OSAS (10.33 ± 1.42) and PSAS (8.11 ± 1.06) totals (P < .001 vs all comparators) and the highest SCAR-Q scores across all domains.
  • Both dual regimens outperformed silicone alone. BTX-A+silicone and fCO2L+silicone had comparable POSAS results, though BTX-A+silicone scored higher on SCAR-Q Appearance and Psychological Impact.
  • No serious adverse events were reported.
Clinical Relevance: Suggests a possible additive benefit from multimodal prevention in head and neck scars, though cost, access to laser and BTX-A, and NHS commissioning limit routine adoption.
Limitations: Small sample and heterogeneous head and neck wounds, with unclear allocation across comparator arms (apparently a few patients per comparison) and only 6 months' follow-up, so findings are preliminary despite the Level 1 label.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Hallmarks of Aesthetic Ageing: A Proposed Tissue-Level Framework for Facial Aging and Precision Regenerative Aesthetics

Cohen S, Thor D, Suwanchinda A et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Narrative review with conceptual framework construction (not a systematic review; no formal search or quality-appraisal methodology reported).
Key Question: Can facial ageing be better explained by a tissue-specific hallmarks framework than by systemic ageing models or isolated phenotypic descriptions?
Key Findings:
  • Ten hallmarks proposed: ECM deterioration, fibroblast senescence, regenerative decline, epigenetic drift, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered intercellular signalling, chronic low-grade inflammation, adipose remodelling, structural support failure, and microvascular decline, arranged in three tiers (molecular/cellular drivers, stromal/regenerative dysfunction, structural outcomes).
  • Six hallmarks were classed as Tier 1 and four as Tier 2 evidence maturity; evidence was weakest for molecular and niche-level processes in deeper facial compartments.
  • Evidence converged most strongly on stromal and regenerative dysfunction, with only selective links to structural outcomes.
Clinical Relevance: May shape future mechanism-informed treatment planning and trial endpoints in regenerative aesthetics, though it has no current implications for NHS practice.
Limitations: The framework is entirely untested prospectively, and its clinical value over standard anatomical and phenotypic assessment remains unproven.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Recombinant Platelet-Derived Growth Factor-BB vs Platelet-Rich Plasma in Aesthetic and Regenerative Medicine: Mechanistic Standardization vs Biologic Heterogeneity

Gould M, Shauly O, Gould DJ · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Structured narrative review (PRISMA 2020/PRISMA-S/SWiM reporting; single-database PubMed search, 36 studies included).
Key Question: How does the evidence for PRP compare with that for recombinant PDGF-BB in aesthetic and regenerative applications, given no direct comparisons exist?
Key Findings:
  • PRP has the broader aesthetic evidence base (meta-analyses: ~+25 to +40 hairs/cm² in hair restoration), but only 12.1% of studies gave reproducible protocols and 26.6% reported final product composition; measured growth factor levels did not consistently predict outcomes.
  • rhPDGF-BB has defined dosing and proven benefit in diabetic wound closure (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.14–2.04), but aesthetic data are limited to controlled studies of 5–12 participants with ≤6 months' follow-up.
  • No head-to-head aesthetic trials exist.
Clinical Relevance: PRP evidence cannot be interpreted reliably without preparation detail, so UK clinicians should treat published PRP outcomes cautiously when counselling patients or considering unlicensed use.
Limitations: Single-database search (PubMed only) with narrative synthesis limits completeness and reproducibility; the agents are not directly comparable.

Aesthetic Surgery Journal

Five-Year Clinical Performance and Patient-Reported Outcomes of Mentor MemoryGel and MemoryShape Breast Implants (GLOW Study)

Alderman A, Caplin D, Wixtrom R et al. · 2026 Nov 06
Study Type: Prospective, multicentre, manufacturer-sponsored cohort study (interim 5-year analysis of a 10-year trial); non-randomised.
Key Question: What are the 5-year safety and patient-reported outcomes of Mentor MemoryGel (round, including Xtra) and MemoryShape (anatomical) implants in breast augmentation and reconstruction?
Key Findings:
  • Primary augmentation cohort, estimated 5-year Baker III/IV capsular contracture: 1.42% (MemoryGel Xtra), 5.16% (MemoryGel non-Xtra), 0.31% (MemoryShape). Implant-related reoperation: 2.9%, 5.49%, 3.37%. Explantation: 5.90%, 6.39%, 4.01%.
  • BREAST-Q satisfaction with breasts, psychosocial and sexual well-being improved significantly from baseline to Year 5 (p<0.001); physical well-being returned to baseline.
  • Cohorts: 2,043 MemoryGel non-Xtra, 289 Xtra, 397 MemoryShape.
Clinical Relevance: Provides longer-term, device-specific complication benchmarks to support implant selection and consent discussions in NHS and private practice.
Limitations: The study was not designed for between-device comparisons, so the apparent differences should not guide implant choice, and the abstract gives no reconstruction-cohort data or detail on loss to follow-up.
